entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Riccardo Petroni (died February 18, 1314) emerged as a formidable figure in the Roman Catholic Church, serving as a cardinal and an eminent jurist during a period of profound political and theological upheaval for the papacy, particularly under Boniface VIII and Benedict XI. His career, spanning the closing decades of the thirteenth century and the early years of the fourteenth, saw him occupy crucial roles in the papal curia, wielding significant influence over ecclesiastical policy and legal interpretation across the global reach of the Church.

Elevated to cardinal-deacon of Sant'Eustachio by Pope Celestine V in 1294, Petroni quickly distinguished himself within the College of Cardinals, becoming a trusted advisor and papal legate. Under Pope Boniface VIII, he undertook sensitive diplomatic missions, including a legation to Tuscany and Romagna in 1295-1296, aimed at pacifying factional strife and asserting papal authority. His judicial acumen was highly valued, contributing to the legal framework that underpinned the papacy's temporal and spiritual claims, particularly during Boniface VIII's clashes with secular rulers like Philip IV of France.

Petroni's legacy lies primarily in his steadfast defense of papal prerogatives and his contributions to the practical application of canon law during a tumultuous era. His participation in the papal conclaves of 1303 and 1304, which elected Benedict XI and Clement V respectively, underscores his continued importance in shaping the Church's leadership. While he did not produce major canonical works, his judicial opinions and administrative actions as a cardinal helped to refine and reinforce the legal structures of the medieval Church, influencing its governance for decades.

His passing in Siena in 1314, just as the papacy's move to Avignon was solidifying, marked the end of an era for a cardinal who had dedicated his life to upholding the Roman see's authority from within its traditional Italian heartland.
